title: Motion Along a Straight Line
summary: One-dimensional motion is described by displacement, velocity, and acceleration. The kinematic equations $v=v_0+at$, $x=x_0+v_0t+\tfrac12at^2$, and $v^2=v_0^2+2a\Delta x$ solve constant-acceleration problems, including free fall.

acceleration.plain: Change in velocity per unit time.

graphs of motion.in_class: Slopes give rates; areas give distances.

concept_sections.heading: Position, velocity, acceleration
concept_sections.explanation: Velocity is how fast position changes; acceleration is how fast velocity changes. Signs indicate direction along the line.

concept_sections.heading: The kinematic equations
concept_sections.explanation: For constant acceleration, three equations connect $x,v,a,t$. Choose the one that omits the quantity you neither know nor want.
math_steps: Pick the equation missing the unwanted variable.

concept_sections.heading: Free fall
concept_sections.explanation: Ignoring air resistance, all objects fall with $a=g\approx9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$. Apply the kinematic equations with that acceleration.
math_steps: Set $a=g$ (downward positive or negative by choice).
Velocity is zero at the top of a rise.

concept_sections.heading: Graphs of motion
concept_sections.explanation: The slope of a position–time graph is velocity; the slope of a velocity–time graph is acceleration; the area under a velocity–time graph is displacement.

concept_sections.heading: Average vs instantaneous
concept_sections.explanation: Average velocity uses total displacement over total time; instantaneous velocity is the value at a single instant. They match only for constant velocity.
math_steps: Average $=\Delta x/\Delta t$ over the trip.
Equal only when velocity is constant.

real_world_examples.title: Reaction and braking distance
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Kinematics finds reaction distance (constant speed) plus braking distance ($v^2=v_0^2+2a\Delta x$).

real_world_examples.title: Dropping keys from a window
real_world_examples.scenario: Keys fall to a friend below.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Free-fall equations give the fall time and catch speed.

real_world_examples.title: A drag race
real_world_examples.scenario: A car accelerates down a strip.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: $x=\tfrac12at^2$ relates the run to the acceleration and time.
